restatements.text: Names the measure the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
Provides the official title of the Act.

Declares findings regarding expected federal funding cuts to Medi-Cal, public education, and food assistance, the financial pressure on the health care safety net, and the concentration of billionaire wealth in California as justification for a one-time wealth tax.
States the Act's intent to protect health care, education, and food assistance funding by imposing a one-time tax on billionaires.

Amends the California Constitution to authorize a one-time tax on the personal property and wealth of California billionaires. It creates the 2026 Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund, allocates 90% of revenues to a Health Account and 10% to an Education and Food Assistance Account, and exempts these revenues from the state's constitutional appropriations limit.

Provides rules for the Reserve Fund, directing the Controller's allocations, capping legislative appropriations at $25 billion annually across both accounts, prohibiting the funds from supplanting existing state funding, and requiring annual reporting by the Department of Finance.
Establishes the name of the statutory part as the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.

Imposes a one-time 5% excise tax on the net worth of California residents with a net worth of $1 billion or more (reduced for those between $1 billion and $1.1 billion), payable with 2026 income taxes or in five annual installments with a deferral charge.
Sets rules for calculating net worth, specifying which debts and liabilities may be deducted, and excluding certain contingent or related-party debts.

Establishes complex valuation methods for different asset types, including presumed valuation formulas for private business interests using book value and profits, and rules for trusts and out-of-state property.

Allows taxpayers whose tax liability exceeds their liquid assets to initiate an Optional Deferral Account (ODA), delaying tax payment until assets are withdrawn or the account is closed, subject to annual reporting of material distributions.
Requires appraisers providing certified appraisals to submit copies to the Franchise Tax Board and establishes penalties for appraisers who substantially overstate or understate valuations.

Apportions 100% of the tax to California based on residency on the tax obligation date, while providing a petition process for alternative apportionment if the standard method violates constitutional limits.
Allows a pro rata credit for net wealth taxes paid to other jurisdictions based on the number of days the taxpayer resided in that jurisdiction during 2026.
Defines key terms, including "applicable individual," "net worth," "tax obligation date" (January 1, 2026), and "valuation date" (December 31, 2026).
Grants the Franchise Tax Board broad authority to adopt regulations to administer the tax, exempting the Board from standard Administrative Procedure Act rulemaking requirements until 2028.
Permits the Legislature to amend the Act by a two-thirds vote, provided the amendments further the Act's purposes.
Contains a severability clause directing courts to preserve the tax imposition, including by reforming specific dates if necessary to cure legal defects.

Imposes severe penalties (20% or 40%) for substantial or gross understatements of tax, authorizes the Franchise Tax Board to hire outside experts, allows the Board to appeal Office of Tax Appeals decisions de novo, and establishes general anti-avoidance rules.
Requires the provisions to be liberally construed to achieve the Act's purposes.

Provides an expedited validation action in Sacramento Superior Court to determine the measure's facial validity, routing any appeals directly to the California Supreme Court and bypassing intermediate appellate courts.
Prohibits taxpayers from taking a state income tax deduction for the net worth tax.
Declares that if this measure appears on the ballot alongside a conflicting billionaire net worth tax measure, the one with more votes prevails entirely.
Grants the measure's proponent, or any citizen if the proponent is absent, legal standing to sue or intervene to defend the Act in court.

evidence.why: It introduces a complex new presumption formula combining accounting book value and a specific multiplier of profits to determine the taxable value of private businesses.

evidence.why: It increases the paperwork and reporting burden on private business entities owned by affected taxpayers by demanding specific accounting and profit metrics.

evidence.why: It creates a massive new state tax liability for qualifying households.

analysis.answer: Current law does not impose a statewide wealth tax on individuals; taxation is based on income, sales, and real property. This measure imposes a one-time 5% excise tax on the net worth of California residents who have assets over $1 billion as of January 1, 2026, creating complex new rules for valuing private businesses, out-of-state property, and trusts.

The text explicitly authorizes up to $50 million in direct startup loans to the Franchise Tax Board. Massive compliance costs will fall on taxpayers to secure certified appraisals and manage reporting. Opportunity costs could include wealthy individuals leaving the state or delaying investments to avoid the tax boundary.

The cost falls exclusively on the approximately 200 California billionaires targeted by the tax. The benefits flow primarily to low-income residents who use Medi-Cal, public schools, and food assistance programs, as well as the healthcare providers and school districts that receive the augmented state funding.

Taxpayers will likely attempt aggressive legal challenges and complex asset restructurings, moving wealth into out-of-state trusts or re-characterizing assets. Some may utilize the Optional Deferral Accounts to indefinitely delay payment on illiquid assets. The Franchise Tax Board will respond by hiring experts and initiating extensive audits to contest asset valuations.

The measure addresses projected multi-billion-dollar federal funding cuts to California's safety net programs and extreme wealth inequality. It attempts to fix this by directly taxing the accumulated assets of billionaires to backfill the state budget. The mechanism may face practical collection hurdles due to the illiquid and movable nature of extreme wealth.

The Franchise Tax Board gains extraordinary new discretionary power to value private assets, assess heavy penalties, and create rules without standard administrative constraints. Proponents of the measure gain the legal standing to defend it in court. The Legislature gains the authority to appropriate up to $25 billion annually from the Reserve Fund.

The revenue and economic impacts of a state-level wealth tax are fiercely disputed. Proponents assert it will raise necessary revenue from a highly concentrated, untaxed pool of wealth without harming the broader economy. Opponents argue it will cause immediate capital flight, widespread tax evasion, and heavy administrative costs, potentially depressing long-term state revenues.

The text allocates up to $50 million for initial administration alone, with ongoing costs fully reimbursed from the tax revenue. Significant portions of early revenue could be absorbed by litigation defense, outside expert hiring, and the complex auditing required to enforce the valuation rules.

Because the core tax structure is embedded in the California Constitution, repealing it requires a subsequent ballot measure. However, the Legislature may amend the statutory provisions by a two-thirds vote, provided the amendments are consistent with and further the Act's purposes.

flags.quote: (k) General anti-avoidance rule. (1) If the Board determines that a transaction or series of transactions lack economic substance, or that a substantial purpose for any transaction or series of transactions was to obtain a tax benefit with respect to this Part that is not intended by the voters or the Legislature
flags.note: Allows the Board to retroactively override transactions based on subjective interpretations of economic substance or voter intent.

flags.quote: (e) Notwithstanding any other law, the Reserve Fund is a special fund, permanently separate and apart from the General Fund
flags.note: Overrides existing state accounting and fund rules.

flags.quote: (c) The Legislature shall have the authority to appropriate up to $22.5 billion each fiscal year from the Billionaire Tax Health Account and up to $2.5 billion each year from the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account.
flags.note: The actual distribution of the tax revenue to specific programs depends on the Legislature exercising its appropriation authority.

flags.quote: (a) The provisions of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, also referred to as "the Act," are severable.
flags.note: Includes a severability clause specifically instructing courts to reform dates to save the tax if necessary.
Sets a rigid, retroactive date for assessing tax residency and obligation.

flags.quote: The Legislature may amend the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, by statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, ifthe statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.
flags.note: Requires a supermajority and limits amendments to those that "further the purposes" of the measure.

flags.quote: (1) Ninety percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Health Account ... (2) Ten percent shall be allocated to the Billionaire Tax Education and Food Assistance Account
flags.note: Bundles funding for distinct policy areas (healthcare, education, and food programs) under a single tax measure.

flags.quote: any citizen of this State may defend the legality of this Act, as provided therein through a validation action or as may otherwise be available, and is authorized to sue directly or intervene
flags.note: Creates a private right of action for any citizen to initiate or intervene in lawsuits to defend the Act.
